Replay

Experimental support envelope

7 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓
On this page ↓
Modes and tested combinationsRecovery and failure policyBounds, not scale promisesAuthoring and performance assessmentSecurity and compatibility boundaries

This is the support assessment for the framework-first implementation as of 2026-09-20. Retain Replay as an experimental library alongside Kit. It has working primitives for the requested multiplayer styles and representative integration evidence. It is not a certified production service, an automatic replacement for Kit, or proof that arbitrary gameplay is deterministic.

Start with getting started, then use the compatibility policy and the exact package contracts below. The framework audit maps implementation gates.

Modes and tested combinations#

Mode Implementation and representative evidence Boundary
Offline value simulation Timeline/pools/RNG; standalone Loot; Godot Hello input, history and recordings All mutable simulation dependencies must be explicit; bounded value storage, not arbitrary node/reference snapshots
Server authority and competitive prediction net + Session/Room; Quickdraw/Claimball, recipient filtering and historical-view tests Authority rules, prediction footprint, action timing and disclosure policies remain authored game decisions
Cooperative owner-driven physics owned, Body2/Body3 and authoritative observations; Slopball and owner Cavecrawl Cooperative trust; Godot contact solving is not deterministic rollback or an anti-cheat proof
Host migration and durable recovery Room/coordinator/leases, private checkpoints; planned/crash, repeat, partition, successor loss, return and cold restore fixtures Requires a reachable trusted coordinator and eligible complete backup; crash loss is bounded by the accepted checkpoint, not zero by definition
Deterministic P2P Fixed-roster runner; native/WASM/Rosetta corpus, participant archives and spectator failover Determinism is established for tested models/targets, not arbitrary floats/physics/callbacks; missing history stalls or fails explicitly
Native provisioned P2P P2P_Party + P2P_Direct; two-player TLS enrollment/pair service and encrypted ENet recovery Convenience owner supports two players. Reachable/forwarded endpoints are configured; no automatic NAT traversal
Browser provisioned P2P P2P_Party + authenticated RTC mesh; independent Chrome profiles and guest/creator archive return Fixed roster; credentials and participant history are separate. Authenticated spectator enrollment is not supplied by this party flow
Dedicated authority Server/Observer infrastructure Room profile; native and Chrome recovery Infrastructure identities/standbys must be provisioned; player-hosted backup disclosure is a different trust choice

ENet gameplay is native. Browser gameplay uses WebRTC; a native ENet peer cannot directly join a browser RTC peer. A common backend/native RTC extension is required for such mixed-platform matches. The shared Transport API does not confer backend availability or network reachability.

Most live integration evidence is macOS arm64 + Godot 4.7.1 and local Chrome. Standalone WASM is executed, not only type-checked, in deterministic/archive/trace fixtures. Rosetta checks another ISA binary on the same Mac; it is not independent x86 hardware, Linux or Windows validation. SQLite adapters currently have native darwin/linux implementations; available source is not proof of deployment on both.

RTC/TURN evidence includes local Coturn relay-only UDP/TCP configurations and real datagram loss/delay tests, including migration. Native service fixtures verify localhost TLS with a test CA. Public WSS certificates, real Internet NAT/relay availability, independent hardware and other browser engines remain deployment acceptance work. See TURN datagram evidence.

Steam's packet/Room lifecycle integration has native ABI and local API-contract tests. Live multi-account Valve networking, lobby UX and SteamGameServer are not validated by those fixtures. They remain experimental integrations, not supported live-network claims. See Steam and Steam Room.

Recovery and failure policy#

Room planned handoff freezes after accepted work settles and transfers an approved final checkpoint. Abrupt takeover uses the newest approved usable checkpoint after authority fencing; it can lose later unreplicated work. Retained, rejected, retired and unknown command outcomes have explicit recovery classifications. Complete authority state must only go to a trusted successor. Public projections are not authority archives. See recovery guarantees.

P2P peers retain simulation/input history; a returning process restores its own compatible participant archive and registers a newer incarnation. The native owner refreshes pair decisions for a replacement connection and rejects retired connection generations. A saved world alone is insufficient.

P2P control outage policy: registration/pair control failure clears Party readiness and prevents new admission. It does not by itself invalidate an already authenticated direct link. A signed denial/invalid registration does retire the native link's keys. The current owner does not automatically reconnect failed background control; after service recovery, the application closes/reopens the party and restores/rejoins using its durable enrollment and participant archive. This deliberate distinction prevents an unreviewed background rebind from changing an active process identity underneath its transport. Continuous automatic control recovery is a follow-up capability, not a claimed guarantee.

A final native test kills the actual service after admission. Party readiness fails after about 10.46 seconds while both existing encrypted links remain live; the peers still match the full reference at tick 1200. See the release receipts.

The service cannot authorize new joins/rebinds while unavailable. Existing-link continuation is not offline revocation awareness. Applications requiring continuous online authorization must choose a stricter session policy.

Bounds, not scale promises#

Surface Enforced implementation bounds
Local timeline 2–4096 history frames; 0–4096 events/tick; complete staged suffix before commit
Authoritative model 1–8 playable seats; 16 peer records including nonplayer connections; 16 queued/recent actions per peer
P2P runner 2–8 participants; 32–1024 history frames; delay + prediction + 2 must fit history; input encoding ≤256 bytes; initialization storage guard 256 MiB
Complete authority checkpoint 1 MiB archive, explicit policy/asset validation; runtime history/transport queues are not serialized
P2P archive 16 MiB maximum; retained input/checksum/history windows remain bounded
Provisioning service Up to 32 resident rooms; fixed P2P rooms 2–8 members; bounded invitation and request budgets
Packet/router 65536-byte Transport ceiling; bounded per-lane buffers, ingress/egress budgets and retention on short receives

These are validation/allocation limits. They do not promise that a maximum-size world or maximum population meets a frame budget. Timeline storage includes both history and replay scratch; server peer/baseline caches add further state copies. Measure the concrete World/input/event types, history, packet settings and target hardware. Profile callbacks must not change simulation or block network progress.

Authoring and performance assessment#

The strongest authoring result is specific: the same paid-revive transfer in isolated Scrapyard variants added the predicate and both wallet assignments to Replay's existing value reducer, reused for prediction and authority. Its feature patch changed 3 files with 11 added physical lines versus Kit's 4 files/19 added lines, and the 72 peer receipts preserved the agreed transfer behavior. These are agent-authored structural measurements, not human productivity or debugging-time proof. A separate existing-family weapon required the same authored resource in both implementations. See revive and weapon.

Costs are mixed. The quiet Cavecrawl comparison measured Replay callbacks around 340–401 µs mean versus Kit's 81–85 µs on one machine, while owner motion had similar local-response ranges and Replay predicted the complete inventory transfer. Subsequent same-binary encoding pairs reduced client application traffic 41.7% and host traffic 30.6%, respectively; they did not demonstrate CPU speedups. See comparison, observations and facts.

The older Scrapyard encounter comparison also measured higher Replay callback and bandwidth costs. Its peak RSS was lower for the Replay host but higher for the Replay client; process-lifetime peaks include startup and cannot be summed as simultaneous memory use. Those historical game/protocol builds are evidence of tradeoffs, not current universal benchmarks. The small 520-byte-world P2P benchmark measured about 19.5–21.4 ms process CPU for two peers over 2400 ticks in accelerated test time. It does not predict full-game rollback cost. See combat and P2P profiling.

The evidence supports trying the complete-world authoring approach and profiling representative workloads. It does not justify replacing Kit everywhere or claiming performance/ergonomic superiority. Keep both implementations available.

Security and compatibility boundaries#

Canonical checksums are not authentication. Plain direct Session/ENet fixtures must not be described as encrypted Internet sessions merely because they use tokens. Use the appropriate authenticated/confidential setup and transport policy. Native P2P pair-link framing uses core cryptographic primitives but is new, experimental framing without independent review or forward secrecy against later enrollment/service-key compromise. Functional packet tests are not certification.

There is no human account system, exactly-once external-effect outbox, arbitrary dynamic reference-graph snapshotter, deterministic Godot physics solver, general NAT service or automatic game-content converter. Those are explicit support boundaries. Full game parity and subjective play-feel superiority remain separate follow-up work under the user's framework-first direction.

Run the smoke command, then the focused integration gate for your selected transport and recovery profile. Pin source and toolchain versions. Future source/API, protocol, content and archive changes must follow compatibility; experimental status does not excuse silently loading incompatible data.
